claim: Mutations in the P53 pathway are a hallmark of human cancer.
source: Mutations in the P53 pathway are a hallmark of human cancer.
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer biology that is supported by established scientific knowledge and is stated in the introduction.

claim: Complete loss of P53 is a frequent event in osteosarcoma.
source: In contrast to P53 point mutations in other cancer, complete loss of P53 is a frequent event in osteosarcoma (OS), the most common cancer of bone.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this pattern in osteosarcoma.

claim: Osteosarcoma is the most common cancer of bone.
source: In contrast to P53 point mutations in other cancer, complete loss of P53 is a frequent event in osteosarcoma (OS), the most common cancer of bone.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about osteosarcoma.

claim: Elevated Pthlh (Pthrp), cAMP levels and signalling via CREB1 are characteristic of both p53-deficient osteoblasts and OS.
source: Here we use murine OS models to demonstrate that elevated Pthlh (Pthrp), cAMP levels and signalling via CREB1 are characteristic of both p53-deficient osteoblasts and OS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including measurements of cAMP levels, gene expression, and protein levels.

claim: Normal osteoblasts survive depletion of both PTHrP and CREB1.
source: Normal osteoblasts survive depletion of both PTHrP and CREB1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing cell survival assays after knockdown of PTHrP and CREB1 in normal osteoblasts.

claim: p53-deficient osteoblasts and OS depend upon continuous activation of the PTHrP-cAMP-CREB1 pathway.
source: In contrast, p53-deficient osteoblasts and OS depend upon continuous activation of this pathway and undergo proliferation arrest and apoptosis in the absence of PTHrP or CREB1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing proliferation arrest and apoptosis following knockdown of PTHrP or CREB1 in p53-deficient cells.

claim: p53-deficient osteoblasts and OS undergo proliferation arrest and apoptosis in the absence of PTHrP or CREB1.
source: In contrast, p53-deficient osteoblasts and OS depend upon continuous activation of this pathway and undergo proliferation arrest and apoptosis in the absence of PTHrP or CREB1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including proliferation assays and AnnexinV/7-AAD staining showing apoptosis.

claim: The PTHrP-cAMP-CREB1 axis is an attractive pathway for therapeutic inhibition in OS.
source: Our results identify the PTHrP-cAMP-CREB1 axis as an attractive pathway for therapeutic inhibition in OS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing the dependence of OS cells on this pathway.

claim: The most prevalent TP53 mutations are point mutations that result in proteins with altered function.
source: The most prevalent mutations are point mutations that result in proteins with altered function (Olivier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: In osteosarcoma, unique genomic rearrangements and other mutation types most often result in null alleles of P53.
source: In osteosarcoma (OS), the most common primary tumour of bone, unique genomic rearrangements and other mutation types most often result in null alleles of P53 (Ribi et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior sequencing studies of osteosarcoma.

claim: OS occurs predominantly in children and teenagers.
source: OS occurs predominantly in children and teenagers and 5 year survival rates have plateaued at ~70% for patients with localised primary disease and ~20% for patients with metastatic or recurrent disease (Janeway et al., 2012; Mirabello et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to epidemiological studies.

claim: 5 year survival rates for OS have plateaued at ~70% for patients with localised primary disease.
source: OS occurs predominantly in children and teenagers and 5 year survival rates have plateaued at ~70% for patients with localised primary disease and ~20% for patients with metastatic or recurrent disease (Janeway et al., 2012; Mirabello et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical outcome studies.

claim: 5 year survival rates for OS are ~20% for patients with metastatic or recurrent disease.
source: OS occurs predominantly in children and teenagers and 5 year survival rates have plateaued at ~70% for patients with localised primary disease and ~20% for patients with metastatic or recurrent disease (Janeway et al., 2012; Mirabello et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical outcome studies.

claim: Sequencing of OS identified the universal mutation of TP53 accompanied by recurrent mutation of RB1, ATRX and DLG2 in 29%-53% of cases.
source: Sequencing of OS using both whole genome and exome approaches identified the universal mutation of TP53 accompanied by recurrent mutation of RB1, ATRX and DLG2 in 29%-53% of cases (Ribi et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2014; Perry et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic sequencing studies.

claim: Trp53+/- and Trp53-/- mice develop OS in addition to other tumors.
source: The OS predisposition of Li-Fraumeni patients and mouse models support the key role of p53 mutation in OS: Trp53+/- and Trp53-/- mice develop OS in addition to other tumors while conditional deletion of Trp53 in the osteoblastic lineage results in full penetrance OS, largely in the absence of other tumor types (Mutsaers and Walkley, 2014; Donehower et al., 1992; Quist et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2006; Lengner et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mouse model studies.

claim: Conditional deletion of Trp53 in the osteoblastic lineage results in full penetrance OS, largely in the absence of other tumor types.
source: The OS predisposition of Li-Fraumeni patients and mouse models support the key role of p53 mutation in OS: Trp53+/- and Trp53-/- mice develop OS in addition to other tumors while conditional deletion of Trp53 in the osteoblastic lineage results in full penetrance OS, largely in the absence of other tumor types (Mutsaers and Walkley, 2014; Donehower et al., 1992; Quist et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2006; Lengner et al., 2006; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mouse model studies.

claim: A GWAS defined two OS susceptibility loci in human: the metabotropic glutamate receptor GRM4 and a region on chromosome 2p25.2 lacking annotated transcripts.
source: A GWAS defined two OS susceptibility loci in human: the metabotropic glutamate receptor GRM4 and a region on chromosome 2p25.2 lacking annotated transcripts (Savage et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a GWAS study.

claim: GRM4 has a role in cAMP generation.
source: GRM4 has a role in cAMP generation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of GRM4 function.

claim: A GWAS in dogs with OS identified variants of GRIK4 and RANK (TNFRSF11A), both involved in cAMP pathways.
source: A GWAS in dogs with OS identified variants of GRIK4 and RANK (TNFRSF11A), both involved in cAMP pathways (Karlsson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a canine GWAS study.

claim: Using a murine OS model induced by an osteocalcin promoter-driven SV40T/t, OS were identified that deleted a regulatory subunit of the cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) complex, Prkar1a, or with amplification of Prkaca, the PKA catalytic component.
source: Using a murine OS model induced by an osteocalcin promoter-driven SV40T/t, OS were identified that deleted a regulatory subunit of the cAMP-dependent protein kinase (PKA) complex, Prkar1a, or with amplification of Prkaca, the PKA catalytic component (Molyneux et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior mouse model study.

claim: A recent transposon mediated mutagenesis OS model recovered both activating and inactivating mutations within cAMP related pathways.
source: A recent transposon mediated mutagenesis OS model recovered both activating and inactivating mutations within cAMP related pathways, but no functional analysis was performed (Moriarity et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a transposon mutagenesis study.

claim: PTHrP and PTH activate their common receptor, PTHR1.
source: PTHrP and PTH activate their common receptor, PTHR1 (Suva et al., 1987; Juppner et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies identifying PTHR1 as the common receptor.

claim: Binding to PTHR1 on osteoblasts or OS cells activates adenylyl cyclase, stimulates cAMP production, followed by PKA activation.
source: Binding to PTHR1 on osteoblasts or OS cells activates adenylyl cyclase, stimulates cAMP production, followed by PKA activation, leading to many of the transcriptional changes associated with PTH/PTHrP treatment (Gardella and Jüppner, 2001; Pioszak and Xu, 2008; Swarthout et al., 2002; Partridge et al., 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of PTHR1 signaling.

claim: In normal osteoblasts PTHrP is produced by osteoblastic lineage cells and acts in a paracrine manner upon other osteoblastic cells at different stages of differentiation.
source: In normal osteoblasts PTHrP is produced by osteoblastic lineage cells and acts in a paracrine manner upon other osteoblastic cells at different stages of differentiation (Martin, 2005; Miao, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of PTHrP function in bone.

claim: The long-term administration of PTH(1–34) resulted in a high incidence of OS in rats.
source: The long-term administration of PTH(1–34) resulted in a high incidence of OS in rats (Vahle et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a rat toxicology study.

claim: Elevated expression of PTHR1 is a feature of human and rodent OS.
source: Elevated expression of PTHR1 is a feature of human and rodent OS (Martin et al., 1976; Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies measuring PTHR1 expression.

claim: PTHrP was expressed in murine OS subtypes.
source: PTHrP was expressed in murine OS subtypes (Ho et al., 2015), placing it as a plausible ligand for activating PTHR1 signaling.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study by the authors.

claim: The consequence of PTH/PTHrP signaling via cAMP-PKA is phosphorylation of the cAMP response element binding (CREB1) protein.
source: The consequence of PTH/PTHrP signaling via cAMP-PKA is phosphorylation of the cAMP response element binding (CREB1) protein (Datta and Abou-Samra, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study of PTH signaling.

claim: CREB1 regulates gene expression through the activation of cAMP-dependent or -independent signal transduction pathways.
source: CREB1 regulates gene expression through the activation of cAMP-dependent or -independent signal transduction pathways (Mayr and Montminy, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of CREB1 function.

claim: Over 20 days culture, a loss of expression of p53 target genes in the KO cultures + tamoxifen occurred, compared to both WT and non-tamoxifen treated isogenic R26-CreERT2ki/+Trp53fl/fl cultures.
source: Over 20 days culture, a loss of expression of p53 target genes in the KO cultures + tamoxifen occurred, compared to both WT and non-tamoxifen treated isogenic R26-CreERT2ki/+Trp53fl/fl cultures (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The expression of CREB1 target genes was increased, inversely paralleling the reduction in p53 target genes.
source: Strikingly, the expression of CREB1 target genes was increased, inversely paralleling the reduction in p53 target genes (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: Loss of p53 was associated with an increase in total CREB1 and phosphorylated CREB1 (pCREB1) in the KO cells.
source: The altered transcript levels were reflected at the protein level, where loss of p53 was associated with an increase in total CREB1 and phosphorylated CREB1 (pCREB1) in the KO cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The KO cultures had increased cAMP levels compared to WT or isogenic controls.
source: Interestingly, the KO cultures had increased cAMP levels compared to WT or isogenic controls (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Derepression of cAMP/CREB1 pathways is an early event following Trp53 mutation in osteoblasts.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that derepression of cAMP/CREB1 pathways is an early event following Trp53 mutation in osteoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased cAMP and CREB1 activity after p53 deletion.

claim: The p53-WT cells were largely unaffected by the shRNA's independent of tamoxifen treatment, except for an initial delayed proliferation in shCreb1 cultures.
source: The p53-WT cells were largely unaffected by the shRNA's independent of tamoxifen treatment, except for an initial delayed proliferation in shCreb1 cultures (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Knockdown of either Creb1 or Pthlh completely prevented the hyperproliferation of the KO + tamoxifen cells.
source: In contrast, knockdown of either Creb1 or Pthlh completely prevented the hyperproliferation of the KO + tamoxifen cells (Figure 1E–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–F).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 1E-F and supplementary figures.

claim: Intact PTHrP and CREB1 signaling are required for the hyperproliferation of p53 deficient osteoblasts.
source: Therefore, intact PTHrP and CREB1 signaling are required for the hyperproliferation of p53 deficient osteoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proliferation data after knockdown experiments.

claim: The p53-KO osteoblasts underwent apoptosis within 48 hr of knockdown with either shCreb1 or shPthlh whilst the isogenic control (-tam) cultures were minimally affected.
source: The p53-KO osteoblasts underwent apoptosis within 48 hr of knockdown with either shCreb1 or shPthlh whilst the isogenic control (-tam) cultures were minimally affected (Figure 1G–H).
evidence: This is supported by AnnexinV/7-AAD staining data shown in Figure 1G-H.

claim: The hyperproliferative effect of loss of Trp53 in osteoblastic cells required PTHrP and CREB1.
source: The hyperproliferative effect of loss of Trp53 in osteoblastic cells required PTHrP and CREB1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proliferation and survival data after knockdown experiments.

claim: Osteoblastic OS cells expressed high levels of Pthlh transcript.
source: Osteoblastic OS cells expressed high levels of Pthlh transcript (Figure 2B), consistent with our previous data identifying substantial levels of intracellular PTHrP in OS cells (Ho et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2B and citation to prior work.

claim: Treatment with a neutralising anti-PTHrP antibody significantly and substantially reduced cAMP levels.
source: Treatment with a neutralising anti-PTHrP antibody significantly and substantially reduced cAMP levels (Onuma et al., 2004) (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP assay data shown in Figure 2C and supplementary figures.

claim: Using the shRNAs against Pthlh, a >50% reduction in the cAMP accumulation was observed.
source: Using the shRNAs against Pthlh, a >50% reduction in the cAMP accumulation was observed (Figure 2D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP assay data shown in Figure 2D-E and supplementary figures.

claim: The reduction of cAMP levels by Pthlh knockdown or by antibody mediated PTHrP neutralization are consistent with OS–derived PTHrP as an endogenous ligand promoting cAMP accumulation.
source: The reduction of cAMP levels by Pthlh knockdown or by antibody mediated PTHrP neutralization are consistent with OS–derived PTHrP as an endogenous ligand promoting cAMP accumulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cAMP data after PTHrP knockdown and antibody treatment.

claim: Knockdown of Pthlh reduced the proliferation of OS cells.
source: Knockdown of Pthlh (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) reduced the proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Knockdown of Pthlh reduced the levels of pCREB1, and surprisingly, total CREB1 in OS cells at early time points post infection.
source: Knockdown of Pthlh (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) reduced the proliferation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), transcription of known target genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F–G) and the levels of pCREB1, and surprisingly, total CREB1 in OS cells at early time points post infection (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the basal expression of CREB1 target genes following Pthlh knockdown.
source: Correspondingly there was a significant reduction in the basal expression of CREB1 target genes (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Primary osteoblasts were largely unaffected by Pthrp knockdown.
source: Primary osteoblasts were largely unaffected by Pthrp knockdown. In contrast there was a rapid induction of apoptosis following Pthlh knockdown in OS cells (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: This is supported by AnnexinV/7-AAD staining data shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: There was a rapid induction of apoptosis following Pthlh knockdown in OS cells.
source: Primary osteoblasts were largely unaffected by Pthrp knockdown. In contrast there was a rapid induction of apoptosis following Pthlh knockdown in OS cells (Figure 2H–I).
evidence: This is supported by AnnexinV/7-AAD staining data shown in Figure 2H-I.

claim: The cells overexpressing high levels of PTHrP failed to thrive and a significant proportion underwent cell death.
source: Surprisingly, the cells overexpressing high levels of PTHrP failed to thrive and a significant proportion underwent cell death indicating that PTHrP overexpression alone is not sufficient to support OS initiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by cell death assay data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: PTHrP overexpression alone is not sufficient to support OS initiation.
source: Surprisingly, the cells overexpressing high levels of PTHrP failed to thrive and a significant proportion underwent cell death indicating that PTHrP overexpression alone is not sufficient to support OS initiation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cell death data after PTHrP overexpression.

claim: Two different fibroblastic OS lines infected with control (sh-Luc) or sh-Pthlh_A were grafted subcutaneously in vivo and both had significantly reduced proliferation as measured by tumor weight.
source: Two different fibroblastic OS lines infected with control (sh-Luc) or sh-Pthlh_A were grafted subcutaneously in vivo and both had significantly reduced proliferation as measured by tumor weight (Figure 2J), comparable to the effects of shPthr1 knockdown in the same OS lines (Ho et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: PTHrP is a critical, OS cell-derived stimulus of the elevated cAMP in OS.
source: These results demonstrate that PTHrP is a critical, OS cell-derived stimulus of the elevated cAMP in OS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the cAMP, proliferation, and survival data after PTHrP manipulation.

claim: OS cells produced significantly greater amounts of intracellular cAMP compared to primary murine osteoblasts.
source: OS cells produced significantly greater amounts of intracellular cAMP compared to primary murine osteoblasts (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP assay data shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: Treatment with the direct cAMP agonist forskolin in the presence of IBMX resulted in an increased and sustained accumulation of cAMP in OS compared to primary osteoblasts.
source: Furthermore, treatment with the direct cAMP agonist forskolin in the presence of IBMX resulted in an increased and sustained accumulation of cAMP in OS compared to primary osteoblasts (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by cAMP kinetics data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Induction of pCREB1 was rapid in normal osteoblasts, peaking at 30 min, then reducing throughout the 120 min time course.
source: Induction of pCREB1 was rapid in normal osteoblasts, peaking at 30 min, then reducing throughout the 120 min time course as expected (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: OS cells displayed continuous and persistent activation of pCREB1.
source: In contrast, OS cells displayed continuous and persistent activation of pCREB1, consistent with the cAMP levels (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The OS-specific altered dynamics of cAMP and pCREB1 resulted in aberrantly extended transcriptional activation of known CREB1 target genes.
source: The OS-specific altered dynamics of cAMP and pCREB1 resulted in aberrantly extended transcriptional activation of known CREB1 target genes based on both transcript expression and chromatin occupancy of CREB1/pCREB1 (Figure 3E–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and ChIP data shown in Figure 3E-F and supplementary figures.

claim: CREB1 was more prominently phosphorylated in the osteoblastic OS than in either the fibroblastic OS or primary osteoblasts.
source: CREB1 was more prominently phosphorylated in the osteoblastic OS than in either the fibroblastic OS or primary osteoblasts (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The mean Creb1 expression was 2–3 fold higher in osteoblastic OS compared to fibroblastic OS and primary osteoblasts.
source: qRT-PCR using independent OS cultures and primary osteoblasts demonstrated that the mean Creb1 expression was 2–3 fold higher in osteoblastic OS compared to fibroblastic OS and primary osteoblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Analysis of RNA-seq from human OS revealed a significant increased in the expression level of Creb1 in OS compared to normal osteoblasts.
source: Analysis of RNA-seq from human OS revealed a significant increased in the expression level of Creb1 in OS compared to normal osteoblasts (Figure 3H) (Moriarity et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3H and citation to prior work.

claim: During culture in differentiation inductive conditions, CREB1 levels reduced over the first 7 days in osteoblasts and stayed low for the remainder of the culture.
source: During culture in differentiation inductive conditions, CREB1 levels reduced over the first 7 days in osteoblasts and stayed low for the remainder of the culture (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3I and supplementary figures.

claim: OS cells maintained CREB1 expression under differentiation conditions.
source: In contrast, OS cells maintained CREB1 expression under the same conditions (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3I and supplementary figures.

claim: The decrease in CREB1 expression (both transcript and protein levels) upon differentiation was confirmed in primary human osteoblasts.
source: The decrease in CREB1 expression (both transcript and protein levels) upon differentiation was confirmed in primary human osteoblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and qPCR data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: There was a 2–3 fold decreased expression of several members of phosphodiesterases (PDE), A kinase anchoring proteins (AKAP) and protein phosphatases (PP) gene families in the murine OS cells compared to primary osteoblasts.
source: There was a 2–3 fold decreased expression of several members of these gene families in the murine OS cells compared to primary osteoblasts (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3J and supplementary figures.

claim: The reduced expression of PDE, AKAPs and PPs would be expected to favour the accumulation and action of cAMP following GPCR activation.
source: The reduced expression of PDE, AKAPs and PPs would be expected to favour the accumulation and action of cAMP following GPCR activation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known functions of these proteins in regulating cAMP levels.

claim: After 72 hr treatment with forskolin, primary osteoblasts had altered cell surface phenotypes and reduced expression of Runx2 and Osx.
source: After 72 hr treatment, primary osteoblasts had altered cell surface phenotypes and reduced expression of Runx2 and Osx (Figure 4A–C) (Mutsaers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: During differentiation, cAMP activation led to decreased expression of differentiation markers and failure to normally mineralise in primary osteoblasts.
source: During differentiation, cAMP activation led to decreased expression of differentiation markers and failure to normally mineralise (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and mineralization assay data shown in Figure 4D-E and supplementary figures.

claim: Continuously elevated cAMP increased features associated with immature osteoblasts.
source: Therefore continuously elevated cAMP increased features associated with immature osteoblasts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differentiation data after forskolin treatment.

claim: In OS cells, the cell surface phenotypes and expression of Runx2 and Sp7 were the inverse of primary osteoblasts after 72 hr forskolin treatment.
source: In OS cells, the cell surface phenotypes and expression of Runx2 and Sp7 were the inverse of primary osteoblasts after 72 hr forskolin treatment (Figure 4F–H, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and qPCR data shown in Figure 4F-H and supplementary figures.

claim: Under differentiation conditions, forskolin induced less profound changes in the expression of markers of osteoblast maturation in OS cells, with the exception of Osteocalcin.
source: Under differentiation conditions, forskolin induced less profound changes in the expression of markers of osteoblast maturation, with the exception of Osteocalcin (Figure 4I), and resulted in increased mineralization (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and mineralization assay data shown in Figure 4I-J and supplementary figures.

claim: Forskolin treatment resulted in increased mineralization in OS cells.
source: Under differentiation conditions, forskolin induced less profound changes in the expression of markers of osteoblast maturation, with the exception of Osteocalcin (Figure 4I), and resulted in increased mineralization (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by mineralization assay data shown in Figure 4J and supplementary figures.

claim: Both early and late markers of maturation were reduced with sh-Creb1 in fibroblastic OS cells.
source: Both early and late markers of maturation were reduced with sh-Creb1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Mineralization was significantly reduced in sh-Creb1 expressing cells compared to controls.
source: Mineralization was significantly reduced in sh-Creb1 expressing cells compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1K–L).
evidence: This is supported by mineralization assay data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Continuously elevated cAMP has distinct effects on the behaviour of normal osteoblasts and OS.
source: Therefore continuously elevated cAMP has distinct effects on the behaviour of normal osteoblasts and OS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differentiation data comparing primary osteoblasts and OS cells.

claim: Loss of CREB1 in primary osteoblasts caused reduced proliferation in the first week then the cells recovered and proliferated similarly to control infected cells thereafter, with no apparent effect on survival.
source: CREB1 knockdown in primary osteoblasts caused reduced proliferation in the first week then the cells recovered and proliferated similarly to control infected cells thereafter, with no apparent effect on survival (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Loss of CREB1 in fibroblastic OS cells resulted in sustained proliferation impairment, yet cell survival was not appreciably impacted.
source: Loss of CREB1 in fibroblastic OS cells resulted in sustained proliferation impairment, yet cell survival was not appreciably impacted (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Knockdown of CREB1 in osteoblastic OS caused profound proliferation arrest and apoptosis.
source: Knockdown of CREB1 in osteoblastic OS, the most common clinical subtype, caused profound proliferation arrest and apoptosis (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation and apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CREB1 is dispensable for normal osteoblast function yet required for proliferation of fibroblastic OS and survival of osteoblastic OS.
source: Therefore, CREB1 is dispensable for normal osteoblast function yet required for proliferation of fibroblastic OS and survival of osteoblastic OS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the proliferation and survival data after CREB1 knockdown.

claim: 32 of the 45 genes from the PTHrP-specific gene signature were most highly expressed in the osteoblastic OS.
source: Using proliferating primary osteoblasts, fibroblastic OS and osteoblastic OS cells, 32 of the 45 genes were most highly expressed in the osteoblastic OS (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Archetypal CREB1 target genes were all more highly expressed in osteoblastic OS.
source: Archetypal CREB1 target genes were all more highly expressed in osteoblastic OS (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B and supplementary figures.

claim: Chromatin immunoprecipitation-PCR (ChIP-qPCR) demonstrated enrichment of active pCREB1 and serine 2 phosphorylated RNA polymerase II (pPolII) on CREB1 target genes in osteoblastic OS.
source: Chromatin immunoprecipitation-PCR (ChIP-qPCR) demonstrated enrichment of active pCREB1 and serine 2 phosphorylated RNA polymerase II (pPolII), a mark of active transcription, on CREB1 target genes in osteoblastic OS (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D) (Ho and Shuman, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C and supplementary figures.

claim: Promoter binding was generally lower in the fibroblastic OS, consistent with the expression patterns of the target genes.
source: Promoter binding was generally lower in the fibroblastic OS, consistent with the expression patterns of the target genes.
evidence: This is an observation from the ChIP-qPCR data.

claim: The enhanced binding of CREB1 in osteoblastic OS corresponded to the elevated levels of cAMP.
source: The enhanced binding of CREB1 in osteoblastic OS corresponded to the elevated levels of cAMP and osteoblastic OS is characterised by increased CREB1 activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP and cAMP data.

claim: Osteoblastic OS is characterised by increased CREB1 activity.
source: The enhanced binding of CREB1 in osteoblastic OS corresponded to the elevated levels of cAMP and osteoblastic OS is characterised by increased CREB1 activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP, cAMP, and gene expression data.

claim: In the top 20 pathways enriched within the somatic SNV mutations of human OS were signatures associated with ion channel complexes, transmembrane transporter complexes, PI3K signaling, calcium channel signaling, and protein kinase A (PKA) activity, all of which are related to cAMP.
source: In the top 20 pathways were signatures associated with ion channel complexes, transmembrane transporter complexes, PI3K signaling, calcium channel signaling, and protein kinase A (PKA) activity, all of which are related to cAMP (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Genes within the cAMP interactome were most highly enriched within the somatic SNV mutations of human OS compared to other cancers.
source: Genes within the cAMP interactome were most highly enriched within the somatic SNV mutations of human OS (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Despite the diverse mutational pattern of somatic SNV mutations in human OS, recurrent and enriched changes in the cAMP and CREB1 pathways occur in OS.
source: These data suggest that, despite the diverse mutational pattern of somatic SNV mutations in human OS, recurrent and enriched changes in the cAMP and CREB1 pathways occur in OS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pathway and enrichment analysis data.

claim: An early consequence of p53 deletion in osteoblastic cells was increased cAMP levels and the autocrine activation of cAMP signalling via PTHrP.
source: We identified that an early consequence of p53 deletion in osteoblastic cells was increased cAMP levels and the autocrine activation of cAMP signalling via PTHrP.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on p53-deficient osteoblasts.

claim: The activation of the PTHrP-cAMP-CREB1 axis was required for the hyperproliferative phenotype of Trp53 deficient osteoblasts and the maintenance of established OS.
source: The activation of the PTHrP-cAMP-CREB1 axis was required for the hyperproliferative phenotype of Trp53 deficient osteoblasts and the maintenance of established OS, identifying this as a tractable pathway for therapeutic inhibition in OS.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data on proliferation and survival.
